name.text: Neural Message Passing for Quantum Chemistry

claim.text: The Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance on all QM9 regression targets, reaching chemical accuracy on 11 of the 13 targets and outperforming prior models such as SchNet and DTNN.
Inference with the MPNN takes roughly 10⁻² seconds per molecule, about 300,000 times faster than the DFT reference calculation (~10³ seconds).
The multiple‑tower architecture reduces the computational complexity of a propagation step from O(n²d²) to O(n²d²/k) and yields a 2× speedup for n=9, d=200, k=8.
A general training method allows MPNNs to use larger node representation dimensions without increasing computation time or memory, providing substantial savings over previous high‑dimensional MPNNs.
Introducing a virtual edge type for pairs of non‑connected nodes enables long‑distance information propagation during message passing.
Adding a latent master node that connects to every atom provides a global scratch space, allowing larger hidden dimensions with minimal performance penalty.

claim_article.text: Using a pair‑message function that depends on both source and destination node states improves message‑passing efficiency compared with the standard matrix‑multiplication message function.
The Message Passing Neural Network framework unifies eight previously proposed graph‑based neural models under a single formalism.
Learning directly from molecular graphs without handcrafted descriptors enables the MPNN to achieve lower prediction errors than descriptor‑based methods.
Across all QM9 properties, the MPNN reduces the mean absolute error by 30–70 % relative to the best previously reported graph‑neural‑network baseline.

problem.text: apply the general MPNN approach to practically important graph problems
automate challenging chemical search problems in drug discovery

name.text: SchNet: A continuous-filter convolutional neural network for modeling quantum interactions

claim.text: Continuous-filter convolutional (cfconv) layers enable convolution on arbitrarily positioned inputs, overcoming the limitations of discrete filters that require grid-aligned data.
SchNet provides rotationally invariant energy predictions and rotationally equivariant, energy‑conserving force predictions by defining forces as the negative gradient of the predicted energy.

When trained on MD17 trajectories with a combined energy‑and‑force loss, SchNet achieves energy MAE ≤0.12 kcal/mol and force MAE ≤0.33 kcal/mol/Å, matching or surpassing GDML and DTNN on all tested molecules, including flexible ones such as malonaldehyde and ethanol.
Training SchNet with forces on only 1,000 examples yields better accuracy than training on 50,000 examples using energies alone, demonstrating that force information improves data efficiency.

On the ISO17 benchmark, SchNet reaches chemical‑accuracy (≈0.5 kcal/mol MAE) for energy predictions on molecules seen during training and further improves predictions on unseen isomers when forces are included in training.
Including force information in the training loss causally improves SchNet’s generalization to previously unseen chemical structures in ISO17.

claim_article.text: GDML cannot be trained on 50,000 MD17 examples due to its quadratic scaling with the number of atoms and samples, whereas SchNet scales to that dataset size.
The ISO17 benchmark, comprising 645,000 conformations of 129 C7O2H10 isomers, is introduced to evaluate models on combined chemical and conformational variation.
Using a shifted softplus activation guarantees an infinitely differentiable (smooth) potential energy surface, facilitating geometry optimization.
Continuous-filter convolutions produce smoother energy predictions than discrete filters, as illustrated in Figure 1.

problem.text: more challenging benchmark with chemical and structural variations
modeling objects with arbitrary positions such as astronomical observations
extending the domain of the machine learning model to both compositional (chemical) and configurational (structural) degrees of freedom
learning a representation for molecules using equilibrium and non‑equilibrium conformations

name.text: Artificial Intelligence for Multiscale Modeling in Solid-State Physics and Chemistry: A Comprehensive Review

claim.text: Artificial intelligence has transformed multiscale modeling by linking atomic, mesoscale, and continuum scales, delivering improved accuracy and reduced computational cost compared with traditional methods.

Machine‑learning‑driven interatomic potentials (e.g., GAP, DeePMD) and DFT‑trained surrogate models enable simulations of up to millions of atoms while retaining accuracy close to first‑principles benchmarks, making large‑scale high‑fidelity simulations feasible.

Neural‑network‑based electronic‑structure prediction tools achieve significant speedups over conventional density‑functional theory while maintaining comparable accuracy, accelerating electronic‑structure calculations.
Graph neural network architectures such as MEGNet and SchNet enhance prediction of phase transitions, defect dynamics, and bulk material properties relative to classical computational approaches.
The multiscale structural complexity measure introduced by Bagrov et al. detects phase transitions in classical spin systems via a sharp extremum in the temperature derivative dC/dT.

Integrating renormalization‑group concepts with machine‑learning architectures has been used to predict transitions to canted antiferromagnetic phases in 3D Ising and Fermi‑Hubbard models, to classify quantum phases, and to recognize complex many‑body phases from raw simulation data.

claim_article.text: Current challenges limiting AI‑driven multiscale modeling include limited data availability, restricted model transferability, and limited explainability.
Future integration of formal renormalization‑group concepts with machine‑learning architectures is a promising direction for modeling systems near criticality or with strong electron correlations.

name.text: MACE: Higher Order Equivariant Message Passing Neural Networks for Fast and Accurate Force Fields

claim.text: MACE uses four-body (higher-order) messages, allowing only two message‑passing layers to achieve converged accuracy, whereas prior equivariant MPNNs required five or six layers.
MACE attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy, achieving lower root‑mean‑square energy and force errors than previous models on the rMD17, 3BPA, and AcAc benchmark suites.

MACE evaluates roughly ten times faster than prior force‑field models for invariant (L=0) architectures and 4–5 times faster for equivariant (L=1,2) architectures, while delivering lower prediction errors.

MACE shows superior extrapolation ability, reducing energy RMSE by about 30 % at 1200 K and 40 % on dihedral‑slice energies for the 3BPA benchmark, and achieving lower errors on geometries far from the training distribution.
On the 3BPA molecule energy profile, MACE predictions are closest to the DFT ground truth across three dihedral slices, outperforming BOTNet and NequIP.
MACE reaches high accuracy rapidly, matching a converged BOTNet model on the 3BPA dataset after roughly 30 minutes of training on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, and trains each benchmark dataset in 2–6 hours.

claim_article.text: The computational cost of MACE scales O(1) with the number of chemical elements because species embeddings are continuous and not included in the tensor‑product contraction, and higher‑order features are implemented via an efficient single‑loop tensor‑contraction algorithm.
By decoupling body‑order from the number of message‑passing iterations, MACE has a small receptive field of approximately 4–5 Å per layer, enabling efficient parallelisation across GPUs.
Increasing the correlation order of messages (ν) steepens the learning‑curve power law, yielding higher data efficiency.

technical.text: Learnable radial basis with Bessel functions

name.text: General framework for E(3)-equivariant neural network representation of density functional theory Hamiltonian

claim.text: DeepH-E3 provides a universal E(3)-equivariant deep-learning framework that exactly preserves Euclidean symmetry of the DFT Hamiltonian, including spin-orbit coupling.

DeepH-E3 predicts DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements with sub‑meV mean absolute error, reducing the error by roughly a factor of two compared with the original DeepH method across diverse material systems.

DeepH-E3 enables accurate electronic‑structure calculations for supercells larger than 10⁴ atoms, reducing computational cost by several orders of magnitude and allowing calculations in minutes on a single GPU versus months on thousands of CPU cores.

DeepH‑E3 reproduces the band structure of magic‑angle twisted bilayer graphene (θ = 1.08°, 11 164 atoms) in excellent agreement with DFT and low‑energy continuum models, correctly capturing the flat bands near the Fermi level.

DeepH‑E3 predicts a spin‑orbit‑coupling‑induced topological quantum phase transition in twisted bilayer Bi₂Te₃, evidenced by band‑gap closing and reopening and a change of the Z₂ invariant from 0 to 1 as SOC strength increases.
DeepH‑E3 attains sub‑meV accuracy after training on only a few hundred DFT calculations of small, non‑twisted structures, demonstrating high data efficiency.

claim_article.text: DeepH‑E3 generalizes across diverse material systems—including graphene, MoS₂, bismuthene, Bi₂Se₃, and Bi₂Te₃—achieving consistently sub‑meV Hamiltonian prediction errors.
The model generalizes to arbitrarily twisted bilayer structures; the mean absolute error of Hamiltonian predictions decreases as the Moiré supercell size grows (or twist angle decreases).

The equivariant architecture handles spin‑orbital Hamiltonians by separating real and imaginary components and applying a change‑of‑basis for half‑integer representations, thereby preserving equivariance without requiring complex‑valued network layers.
The model can fit 2.8 × 10⁹ non‑zero complex‑valued Hamiltonian matrix elements with only ~10⁵ real trainable parameters, indicating high capacity efficiency.

problem.text: Construction of a Moiré‑twisted material database using DeepH‑E3
Extension of E(3)‑equivariant neural networks to capture DeepH’s small‑to‑large scale learning capability
Optimization of local coordinate selection to reduce computational load in equivariant models

name.text: Phonon predictions with E(3)-equivariant graph neural networks

claim.text: Phonax efficiently predicts phonon dispersion relations and density of states for inorganic crystal materials.

Including Hessian (second‑derivative) data in training improves the energy model accuracy beyond training with only energy and force data, reduces force MAE, and provides an effective ~7× increase in the amount of force information.
Augmenting a minimal 1×1×1 supercell training set with Hessian data yields more accurate phonon predictions than training on a larger 3×3×3 supercell alone.
The E(3)-equivariant graph neural network architecture automatically preserves crystalline symmetries, yielding the correct acoustic‑sum‑rule zero modes without additional corrections.
Phonax can predict molecular vibrational spectra and correctly assign IR/Raman active modes by analyzing irreducible representations.
Fine‑tuning an energy model on a benzene vibrational spectrum improves spectrum predictions for unseen molecules such as toluene and phenol.

claim_article.text: A generalized energy model that includes external electric‑field dependence can predict polarization, Born effective charges, and polarizability, and improves energy and force MAE.
The Phonax framework works for both periodic crystals and isolated molecules and can be extended to higher‑order derivatives such as field‑dependent properties.

problem.text: Generalized energy models that include external fields
High‑throughput AI‑guided material design frameworks incorporating phonon predictions
Application of equivariant GNN phonon predictions to drug‑discovery related molecular systems
Extension of Hessian‑based training to other higher‑order physical observables

name.text: GNN-Assisted Phase Space Integration with Application to Atomistics

claim.text: Standard Gaussian quadrature rules produce frame‑dependent (non‑objective) phase‑averaged internal energies for rotated crystal lattices.
Gaussian quadrature leads to abrupt energy jumps and fictitious minima when neighbor cut‑off radii change during large deformations.
Third‑order Gaussian quadrature fails to approximate phase‑space integrals for bulk aluminum above 300 K, producing spurious minima in the Helmholtz free‑energy landscape.
Fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature yields internal energies and free‑energy curves that remain in good agreement with molecular dynamics results across the full temperature range studied.
An E(3)‑equivariant graph neural network architecture guarantees rotational invariance of predicted phase‑averaged quantities.

The E(3)‑equivariant GNN surrogate provides superior accuracy compared with third‑ and fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature for thermal expansion of copper, martensitic phase transition of iron, and grain‑boundary energy calculations, matching molecular dynamics reference data.

claim_article.text: The GNN surrogate achieves mean absolute errors of ≤0.313 meV for energy, ≤0.189 meV/Å for forces, and ≤0.0734 meV/Å² for thermal forces on validation sets.

Inference with the trained GNN is significantly faster than evaluating fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature, enabling frequent high‑dimensional integral evaluations and quasistatic finite‑temperature atomistic simulations without costly MD averaging.
Training the GNN on high‑fidelity Monte‑Carlo integration data enables accurate prediction of phase‑averaged energies and their derivatives for atomic clusters.
The GNN‑assisted integration framework can be applied to high‑dimensional integration problems beyond atomistics.

problem.text: Application of GNN‑assisted phase‑space integration to financial mathematics (e.g., pricing of derivatives)
Extension of the method to dynamic reinforcement learning problems involving high‑dimensional state spaces
Use of the framework for high‑dimensional integrals in quantum physics (multi‑particle Schrödinger equation)
Adapting the technique for data‑mining and large‑scale statistical inference tasks

technical.text: Supervised training of the GNN on phase‑averaged quantities

name.text: Predicting ionic conductivity in solids from the machine-learned potential energy landscape

claim.text: The frozen-framework PES descriptor screening ranks lithium-containing Materials Project compounds such that eight of the ten highest‑ranked materials are confirmed to be room‑temperature superionic conductors by first‑principles calculations.

The proposed screening method is approximately 50 × faster than molecular dynamics driven by a machine‑learning interatomic potential and at least 3 000 × faster than first‑principles molecular dynamics.

The combined descriptor Ξ, defined as the product of sigmoid‑transformed connected and disconnected free‑volume descriptors at a 0.5 eV threshold, achieves higher ranking scores than each individual descriptor and far exceeds random‑guess performance.

Free‑volume (FV) descriptors evaluated at energy thresholds between 0.3 eV and 0.5 eV consistently outperform or match the minimal percolation energy (MPE) descriptor across all three evaluation scores.

Using the frozen‑framework approximation, where only a single Li ion moves while the host lattice remains fixed, reduces the generalization error of the ML‑IAP compared with fully relaxed MD or NEB simulations.

AIMD simulations of the five top‑Ξ candidates confirm high ionic conductivities (e.g., Li(BH)6 shows σ ≈ 0.9 S cm⁻¹ at 1000 K with activation energy 219 ± 86 meV), validating the screening predictions.

claim_article.text: The screening pipeline, when applied to 5 997 lithium‑containing Materials Project structures that satisfy basic stability and band‑gap criteria, yields 1302 structures after removing transition‑metal containing compounds, of which 113 have Ξ > 0.25.
The proposed descriptor‑based screening approach is not tied to a specific ML‑IAP; it can be employed with any universal interatomic potential model.
All evaluated descriptors (MPE, FV‑connected, FV‑disconnected) achieve ranking scores above those of a random‑guess classifier, demonstrating predictive capability for ionic conductivity.

Finite‑size tests using a larger supercell and an ML‑IAP (SevenNet) show that diffusion coefficients converge within statistical uncertainties, confirming that the AIMD results are not significantly affected by supercell size.

task.text: Ranking lithium‑containing crystals for ionic conductivity

problem.text: Development of more generalizable universal interatomic potentials for diverse crystal chemistries
Integration of advanced graph neural network architectures to improve screening speed and accuracy
Scaling heuristic descriptor‑based screening to the entire Materials Project database and beyond
Combining machine‑learned potentials with experimental validation pipelines for superionic material discovery

name.text: Machine Learning-Guided Discovery of Temperature-Induced Solid-Solid Phase Transitions in Inorganic Materials

claim.text: A graph convolutional neural network predicts vibrational free energies with root‑mean‑square errors of 8.23 meV/atom (training), 11.34 meV/atom (validation) and 12.31 meV/atom (test), and its predictions for MgS and NaH polymorphs match DFT‑computed values across the 200–700 K range.

Screening of approximately 50 000 inorganic crystals with the machine‑learning model identified over 2 000 temperature‑induced solid‑solid polymorphic transitions between 300 K and 600 K, including 130 stable transitions within the technologically relevant 300 K–350 K interval.

Twenty‑one stable polar‑nonpolar transitions are predicted to exhibit relative lattice‑thermal‑conductivity changes of at least 20 % (0.20), ranging up to a 73 % increase for ZrSeO with a conductivity ratio of 1.73.

Several predicted solid‑solid transitions show large entropy changes exceeding 300 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹ (e.g., Li₃MnF₇: 342.3 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹, PnCl₂: 338.3 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹, Fe₄OF₇: 252.1 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹), while the highest entropy changes (> 400 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹) are limited to transitions above 450 K and occur exclusively in nonpolar‑nonpolar categories, reducing their relevance for room‑temperature applications.

The presented workflow enables high‑throughput prediction of temperature‑induced solid‑solid phase transitions without performing explicit phonon calculations for each material, dramatically reducing computational cost.

Validation against experimental reports and independent first‑principles calculations confirms the robustness and predictive power of the ML‑guided framework, with reasonable agreement for transition temperatures of KNO₃, KNO₂ and CaCO₃, DFT‑calculated free‑energy differences matching ML predictions for a ten‑material subset, and thermal‑conductivity ratios for Li₄TiS₄ and NaNO₃ closely reproduced by DFT.

claim_article.text: Uncertainty quantification based on latent‑space Euclidean distance provides error estimates that correlate with prediction errors, allowing exclusion of transitions whose uncertainty exceeds 50 % of the absolute free‑energy difference.

Polar‑nonpolar and polar‑polar transitions are more numerous than nonpolar‑nonpolar ones, with 214 polar‑nonpolar, 173 polar‑polar and 228 nonpolar‑nonpolar stable transitions predicted in the 300 K–600 K range.
Metastable phase transitions outnumber stable transitions across all symmetry categories in the screened dataset.
Across the screened temperature range, a larger number of predicted stable phase transitions is generally associated with smaller phase‑transition entropy changes.

task.text: High‑throughput prediction of temperature‑induced solid‑solid phase transitions

name.text: Bridging scales with Machine Learning: From first principles statistical mechanics to continuum phase field computations to study order-disorder transitions in LixCoO2

claim.text: A Hubbard U parameter of 2.5 eV in DFT+U (with a vdW‑DF exchange‑correlation functional) reproduces the experimental average lithiation voltages of LiCoO₂ across the composition ranges {0‑1}, {0‑0.5}, and {0.5‑1}.

A cluster expansion fitted to 333 DFT‑computed LiCoO₂ configurations using a genetic‑algorithm‑guided sparse regression achieves a root‑mean‑square error of 2.49 meV per primitive cell under 10‑fold cross‑validation and accurately reproduces formation energies, especially for configurations on or near the convex hull.
Large‑scale DFT calculations estimate the coherent anti‑phase boundary energy between the η₁ = ½ and η₃ = ½ ordered LiCoO₂ rotational variants to be 30.9 mJ m⁻².

Integrable Deep Neural Networks trained on derivative (chemical‑potential) data accurately learn the high‑dimensional free‑energy density and chemical‑potential functions for LiₓCoO₂, achieving mean‑squared errors comparable to the reported minima and reproducing DFT formation energies with a mean absolute error below 5 meV atom⁻¹.
Using the IDNN reduces the computational cost of generating free‑energy data for continuum models by approximately two orders of magnitude compared with direct DFT sampling.

Phase‑field simulations using the IDNN‑derived free‑energy density predict nucleation rates of the ordered phase at 260 K that are an order of magnitude higher than at 300 K, consistent with a larger free‑energy decrease (1 meV vs 0.5 meV per unit cell).

claim_article.text: The presented scale‑bridging framework, linking DFT‑informed statistical mechanics to continuum phase‑field models via IDNN‑learned free‑energy functions, constitutes the first systematic implementation of this kind for LiCoO₂ cathodes.
Semi‑Grand Canonical Monte Carlo simulations predict an order‑disorder transition temperature slightly above 330 K for the x≈0.5 zig‑zag ordering, in agreement with experimental observations.

Monte Carlo simulations predict an additional ordered phase at Li composition x ≈ 1/3 that becomes stable below roughly 235 K, a phenomenon not observed at room temperature but reported in low‑temperature experiments.
Inclusion of van der Waals interactions together with DFT+U improves the accuracy of predicted order‑disorder transition temperatures for LiCoO₂ relative to earlier first‑principles studies.

name.text: Matbench Discovery: A framework to evaluate machine learning crystal stability predictions

claim.text: EquiformerV2+DeNS (a universal interatomic potential) achieves the highest classification performance among all evaluated models, with F1 scores up to 0.983, ROC AUC 0.96, and discovery acceleration factors up to 6.33, establishing state‑of‑the‑art for ML‑guided materials discovery.

Training universal interatomic potential models with forces, stresses, and magnetic moments substantially improves stability‑prediction performance compared with energy‑only models, enhancing both classification metrics (F1, DAF) and regression metrics (MAE, RMSE).

Regression‑based metrics such as MAE, RMSE, and R² are poorly aligned with classification‑based metrics needed for materials‑discovery tasks, and improvements in these regression metrics do not necessarily translate into higher F1 or discovery acceleration scores.

The WBM test set contains 215,488 unique prototype structures (32,942 thermodynamically stable), is enriched in actinides, lanthanides, metalloids and noble‑transition metals while under‑representing oxygen, is dominated by ternary phases (~75 %), and most structures have fewer than 100 atomic sites, contrasting with the Materials Project training distribution.

Prospective benchmarking that introduces covariate shift between training and test distributions provides a more realistic indicator of real‑world discovery performance than retrospective split strategies, and requires training and test sets larger than the training set to evaluate model scalability.
Random‑forest models excel on small datasets but are outperformed by neural‑network models on large datasets due to the benefits of representation learning.

claim_article.text: Optimizing hyperparameters solely for the Matbench Discovery benchmark may degrade performance of models intended for general‑purpose use.
Models trained on Materials Project data systematically underpredict convex‑hull distances because the training set is biased toward low‑formation‑energy (stable) structures.
High disagreement among model predictions (large standard deviation) can be used to flag potential DFT relaxation failures in high‑throughput screenings.
Accurate regression models can still produce high false‑positive rates near the 0 eV/atom convex‑hull decision boundary.

Stable vs. unstable classification for high‑throughput screening

name.text: E(3)-Equivariant Graph Neural Networks for Data-Efficient and Accurate Interatomic Potentials

claim.text: NequIP achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the MD-17 benchmark, surpassing invariant GNN‑IPs, shallow neural networks, and kernel‑based methods.
NequIP outperforms kernel‑based approaches such as sGDML and FCHL19/GPR across benchmarks, including small-data regimes and the MD-17 dataset.
NequIP requires up to three orders of magnitude fewer training configurations than existing neural interatomic potentials to reach comparable accuracy.
When trained on only 133 structures (~1 k frames), NequIP outperforms DeepMD trained on 133,500 structures for liquid water and ice simulations.
Using higher-order E(3)-equivariant representations (increasing rotation order from l=0 to l=1 and up to l=3) consistently reduces prediction error and improves accuracy across all evaluated tasks.
Predicting forces as the negative gradient of the learned total energy guarantees energy conservation and rotation‑equivariant forces.

claim_article.text: The equivariant architecture scales linearly with the number of atoms because convolutions are limited to a local cutoff radius.
NequIP attains chemical‑accuracy energy errors (~2 meV) on CCSD(T) benchmark molecules using only 1,000 reference configurations, outperforming sGDML and GemNet.
NequIP reproduces structural and kinetic properties from ab‑initio molecular dynamics simulations with high fidelity.

name.text: A SURVEY OF AI FOR MATERIALS SCIENCE: FOUNDATION MODELS, LLM AGENTS, DATASETS, AND TOOLS

claim.text: Foundation models enable cross-domain generalization and emergent capabilities for scientific discovery in materials science.
GNoME discovered over 2.2 million new stable inorganic materials and more than 45 000 new crystal prototypes, an order‑of‑magnitude increase over prior discovery efforts.
MACE‑MP‑0 attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for periodic systems while preserving equivariant inductive biases.

Multimodal models such as nach0, MultiMat, and MatterChat demonstrate reasoning over combined structural, textual, and spectral data, whereas most current foundation models remain unimodal and lack integrated image, spectrum, and experimental‑metadata fusion.

Current foundation models in materials science suffer from limited generalizability, interpretability, data imbalance, safety concerns, inability to model long‑range interactions (electrostatics, dispersion, magnetism), and lack of synthesizability, phase‑stability, or safety constraints, restricting experimental feasibility of generated candidates.

The survey proposes a task‑driven taxonomy that organizes foundation models into six application areas: data extraction/interpretation/Q&A, atomistic simulation, property prediction, materials structure/design/discovery, process planning/discovery/optimization, and multiscale modeling.

claim_article.text: LLM‑based agents such as HoneyComb, LLMatDesign, ChatMOF, MatAgent, and MatPilot have been developed to automate literature search, hypothesis generation, synthesis planning, and experimental verification in materials science.

Existing materials datasets are heavily skewed toward inorganic atomistic systems, with limited coverage of polymers, composites, and mesoscale phenomena, creating a critical data imbalance for foundation‑model training.

Future research should focus on scalable pretraining, continual learning, data governance, trustworthiness, and incorporation of physics‑informed constraints such as equivariance, quantum‑mechanical symmetries, and thermodynamic principles to improve accuracy, interpretability, and trustworthiness of foundation models.

The autonomous A‑Lab platform synthesized 41 of 58 targeted materials (71 % success) over a 17‑day experiment with minimal human intervention, demonstrating high‑throughput autonomous materials synthesis.

name.text: A Universal Graph Deep Learning Interatomic Potential for the Periodic Table

claim.text: The final M3GNet interatomic potential achieves test mean absolute errors of 0.035 eV/atom for energy, 0.072 eV/Å for forces, and 0.41 GPa for stresses on a held‑out Materials Project dataset covering 89 elements.
Relaxing test crystals with M3GNet reduces median volume error from 2.4 % to 0.6 % and energy mean absolute error from 0.169 eV/atom to 0.035 eV/atom relative to DFT‑relaxed references.

A single‑CPU M3GNet relaxation completes in about 22 seconds, compared with 15 hours on 32 cores for DFT; pre‑relaxation with M3GNet shortens subsequent DFT relaxation time by roughly a factor of three and reduces total CPU time by an average factor of 2.97.

Screening 31.7 million hypothetical crystals with M3GNet identifies approximately 1.8 million candidates with predicted hull distances below 0.001 eV/atom, and among the 2,000 lowest‑energy candidates, 1,578 are confirmed stable (Ehull < 0.001 eV/atom) by DFT.

Training M3GNet on energies alone (M3GNet‑E) yields force and stress mean absolute errors larger than the intrinsic data dispersion, demonstrating that forces and stresses must be included in training.
A single universal M3GNet model trained simultaneously on six elements attains error metrics comparable to element‑specific M3GNet models.

claim_article.text: M3GNet predicts phonon band structures and densities of states for SiO₂ polymorphs that quantitatively agree with DFT calculations, and the predicted phonon density‑of‑states center follows the expected ω ∝ 1/√m trend across materials.

M3GNet molecular‑dynamics simulations of Li₃YCl₆ reproduce ionic conductivity (14.3 mS cm⁻¹) and activation energy (0.22 eV) consistent with ab‑initio MD, and short‑time MD correctly identifies known lithium superionic conductors by their high mean‑squared displacements at elevated temperatures.

On the MD17 and MD17‑CCSD(T) molecular force‑field benchmarks, M3GNet achieves lower energy and force errors than the Embedded Atom Neural Network and comparable accuracy to state‑of‑the‑art message‑passing and equivariant neural networks; when benchmarked against quantum‑accurate CCSD/CCSD(T) data, it attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for several molecules.

Across nine MatBench structural property datasets, M3GNet yields lower mean absolute errors than MODNet, AtomSets‑V1, MEGNet, and AutoMatminer, with improvements of 20.5 %–41.3 % on large datasets such as perovskite formation energy and MP band gap, and demonstrates excellent prediction accuracy on the broader MatBench suite.

problem.text: Exploiting intermediate PES data (energies, forces, stresses) from high‑throughput relaxations to further improve IAP accuracy
Extending universal IAP coverage beyond the current 89 elements to the full periodic table
Integrating M3GNet predictions with experimental synthesis validation workflows
Applying M3GNet to discover materials with targeted exceptional properties such as superconductivity or high‑energy‑density battery electrodes

name.text: CHGNet: Pretrained universal neural network potential for charge-informed atomistic modeling

claim.text: CHGNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Matbench Discovery benchmark, outperforming eight other submitted models.

On the Materials Project Trajectory test set, CHGNet trained with magnetic moment labels attains mean absolute errors of 30 meV/atom for energy, 77 meV/Å for forces, 0.348 GPa for stress, and 0.032 µB for magnetic moments.

CHGNet molecular dynamics simulations of Li superionic conductors reproduce room‑temperature ionic conductivities and activation energies within the error bars of AIMD, correctly distinguishing faster from slower conductors.
CHGNet integrates magnetic moment labels as a proxy for atomic charge, enabling inference of atomic charges and accurate differentiation of oxidation states such as V³⁺/V⁴⁺ and Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺.

In charge‑informed molecular dynamics of Li₀.₅MnO₂ at 1100 K, CHGNet predicts the emergence of Mn²⁺ after ~0.8 ns, coinciding with a ~50 meV/oxygen reduction in potential energy and the formation of a spinel‑like phase, indicating a correlation between charge disproportionation and phase transformation.

Including electronic entropy via charge‑decorated cluster expansions, CHGNet reproduces the experimentally observed miscibility gap and eutectoid‑like transition in the LiₓFePO₄ phase diagram, whereas a non‑charge‑decorated model fails to capture these features.

claim_article.text: CHGNet accurately predicts the dramatic increase in Li‑ion diffusivity and the reduction of activation energy (~160 meV) in slightly Li‑stuffed Li₃La₃Te₂O₁₂, matching DFT‑computed values and the activated diffusion network theory.
Fine‑tuning the pretrained CHGNet on the Li‑Fe‑P‑O chemical space reduces the test error from 23 meV/atom to 15 meV/atom.
CHGNet captures long‑range interactions up to 20 Å with only four atom‑convolution layers while maintaining low computational cost.
CHGNet enables nanosecond‑scale molecular dynamics simulations of garnet Li₃La₃Te₂O₁₂, yielding lithium self‑diffusion coefficients with quantified uncertainty.

name.text: Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics: a scalable model with the accuracy of quantum mechanics

claim.text: DeePMD reproduces AIMD energies, forces, and virial tensors for water and ice with root‑mean‑square errors of approximately 1 meV per molecule for energy, 40 meV Å⁻¹ for forces, and 1–2 meV for the virial.
DeePMD accurately reproduces radial distribution functions and three‑body angular distribution functions of liquid water and ice, matching AIMD results.
For a diverse set of organic molecules, DeePMD achieves lower mean absolute errors in both energy and forces than the GDML benchmark.
The computational cost of DeePMD scales linearly with the number of atoms and is several orders of magnitude lower than equivalent AIMD simulations, comparable to empirical force fields.
A DeePMD model trained on relatively small systems (64–96 water or ice molecules) can be directly applied to much larger systems without loss of accuracy, demonstrating strong transferability.
DeePMD preserves translational, rotational, and permutational symmetries by constructing a local reference frame for each atom and sorting neighbor lists by species and inverse distance.

claim_article.text: Using a loss function with adaptive prefactors that emphasize forces early and energies/virial later reduces the total training time to a few core‑hours for all test cases.
Discontinuities in forces caused by the sharp cutoff radius and neighbor‑list sorting are much smaller than thermal fluctuations and do not impair canonical sampling.
In principle, DeePMD could be trained on chemically accurate data from high‑level quantum chemistry or quantum Monte Carlo, extending its applicability beyond density‑functional theory.

problem.text: Efficient training of interatomic potentials with forces and virial regularization

name.text: Deep-Learning Density Functional Theory Hamiltonian for Efficient ab initio Electronic-Structure Calculation

claim.text: DeepH predicts DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements for graphene with an average mean absolute error of 2.1 meV and a coefficient of determination r² = 0.9994 across all orbital combinations.
When applied to unseen graphene configurations sampled between 100 K and 400 K, DeepH maintains a mean absolute error of 1.9 meV for Hamiltonian matrix elements.
For monolayer MoS₂, DeepH predicts DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements with average mean absolute errors of 1.3 meV (Mo–Mo), 1.0 meV (Mo–S), 0.7 meV (S–Mo), and 0.8 meV (S–S).
Band structures and electric susceptibility computed from DeepH for MoS₂ match DFT results closely.
DeepH generalizes to carbon nanotubes, achieving Hamiltonian prediction MAE below 3.5 meV for diameters larger than 2 nm and accurately reproducing their band structures.
DeepH scales linearly with system size and provides a three‑order‑of‑magnitude speed‑up over conventional DFT for a MoS₂ 35 × 35 supercell.

claim_article.text: A DeepH model trained only on non‑twisted bilayer graphene structures predicts Hamiltonians for twisted bilayer graphene supercells up to ~1000 atoms with sub‑meV mean absolute error and correctly reproduces the flat‑band feature near the Fermi level at the magic angle (~1.08°).
DeepH accurately predicts DFT Hamiltonians and electronic properties for twisted bilayer bismuthene with strong spin‑orbit coupling, achieving errors comparable to those for twisted graphene.
Compared with empirical tight‑binding and continuum models, DeepH offers higher accuracy and transferability for twisted van‑der‑Waals materials, albeit with slightly lower computational efficiency.
DeepH resolves the accuracy‑efficiency dilemma of DFT, enabling efficient ab‑initio electronic‑structure calculations for large‑scale material systems.

name.text: Deep-learning electronic-structure calculation of magnetic superstructures

claim.text: xDeepH achieves sub‑meV mean absolute error on DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements for the test set of CrI3 configurations.
xDeepH accurately reproduces DFT band structures of (16,16) CrI3 nanotubes for both non‑collinear surface‑normal magnetization and collinear ferromagnetism.
xDeepH accurately predicts the band structure of monolayer NiBr2 with a 19×1×1 spin‑spiral magnetic order, matching DFT results.
xDeepH generalizes to Moiré‑twisted bilayer CrI3 at a twist angle of 81.79°, a configuration not seen during training, reproducing band structures and density of states in agreement with DFT.

xDeepH reduces the computational cost of electronic‑structure calculations relative to conventional constrained DFT, enabling simulations of magnetic superstructures containing thousands of atoms, such as a 4,336‑atom skyrmion supercell.
Embedding the full E(3) × {I, T} equivariance into the neural‑network architecture reduces the amount of training data required and improves prediction accuracy.

claim_article.text: Introducing magnetic moments via a strictly localized magnetic‑moment layer yields more efficient and accurate training than treating atomic and magnetic structures on equal footing.

The DFT Hamiltonian H_DFT({R},{M}) obeys nearsightedness with two distinct length scales: RN2 ≈ R_C for magnetic‑structure influence and RN1 several times larger for atomic‑structure influence, as confirmed by numerical experiments.

The time‑reversal symmetry of the DFT Hamiltonian is enforced by assigning a parity index t to equivariant vectors, ensuring Hamiltonian sub‑blocks transform correctly under the anti‑unitary T operation.
The ENN architecture of xDeepH preserves equivariance under the Euclidean and time‑reversal symmetry group E(3)×{I,T}, which is essential for the method's performance.

name.text: D4FT: A DEEP LEARNING APPROACH TO KOHN-SHAM DENSITY FUNCTIONAL THEORY

claim.text: The QR‑based reparameterization used in D4FT preserves the orthonormal constraints of Kohn‑Sham orbitals, making the search space equivalent to the original orthogonal function space, as proved in Proposition 3.1, and can be interpreted as projected gradient descent on the orthogonal constraint set.

Direct minimization of the total KS‑DFT energy with stochastic gradient descent reduces the asymptotic computational complexity from O(N⁴) to O(N³), and the full‑batch D4FT algorithm has complexity O(nN²)+O(n²N²), which is lower than the O(n²N²) complexity of conventional SCF; minibatch training further lowers the cost.
D4FT converges to a self‑consistent Kohn‑Sham solution that satisfies the eigenfunction condition.
Across a benchmark set ranging from He to benzene, D4FT reproduces ground‑state energies of the reference PySCF implementation with deviations ≤0.02 Ha (LSDA/6‑31g and LSDA/STO‑3g).
D4FT correctly predicts the paramagnetic ground state of O₂ and the diamagnetic ground state of CO₂ by comparing spin‑restricted and spin‑unrestricted calculations.
D4FT scales to carbon clusters up to C₁₈₀, achieving wall‑clock runtimes an order of magnitude faster (≈1100 s for C₁₈₀) than PySCF, GPAW, Psi4, and JAX‑SCF.

claim_article.text: Incorporating a neural local scaling transformation as a learnable basis (preserving the overlap matrix) enhances wave‑function expressiveness and yields lower LSDA ground‑state energies for atoms (He, Li, Be, C, N, O) compared with the raw STO‑3g basis.
D4FT converges faster than JAX‑SCF, demonstrating a smaller computational complexity and reduced number of iterations.
D4FT provides a unified optimization algorithm with a stronger convergence guarantee than traditional SCF fixed‑point iteration.
D4FT successfully converges on unstable fullerene fragments (C₁₂₀, C₁₄₀) where PySCF fails to converge within the default iteration limit.

name.text: Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Networks for an Accurate and Interpretable Prediction of Material Properties

claim.text: The modified convolution function reduces the mean absolute error for formation‑energy prediction from 0.112 eV/atom to 0.039 eV/atom, achieving DFT‑level accuracy comparable to the experimental DFT‑experiment error of 0.081–0.136 eV/atom.
CGCNN classifies metals versus semiconductors with an area under the ROC curve of 0.95 and an overall accuracy of 0.90.

By extracting per‑atom site energies in perovskites, the model reveals that large‑radius elements stabilize the A site and group 4‑6 elements stabilize the B site, and using these insights the high‑throughput search space for stable perovskites is reduced by a factor of seven (from 18,928 to 228 candidates).

When applied to a set of 1,585 crystals with elastic properties, CGCNN predicts bulk modulus with a mean absolute error of 0.077 log(GPa) and shear modulus with a mean absolute error of 0.114 log(GPa), demonstrating good generalization.
Using roughly 10⁴ training examples, CGCNN attains DFT‑level accuracy for eight distinct material properties across diverse crystal types and compositions.

Compared with a prior statistical‑learning approach, CGCNN achieves similar or lower root‑mean‑square errors for bulk modulus (0.075 log(GPa) vs 0.105) and shear modulus (0.127 log(GPa) vs 0.138) using the same training data.

claim_article.text: Representing crystals as graphs of atoms and bonds provides a universal, size‑invariant input format applicable to any periodic crystal system.

name.text: Graph Networks as a Universal Machine Learning Framework for Molecules and Crystals

claim.text: MEGNet models achieve lower mean absolute errors than SchNet on 11 of the 13 QM9 molecular properties evaluated.

Simple MEGNet models that use only atomic number and spatial distance as input achieve chemical accuracy, perform comparably to full‑feature models, and outperform prior state‑of‑the‑art models on 8 of the 13 QM9 properties.

MEGNet models trained on approximately 60,000 crystals outperform prior models (SchNet and CGCNN) for formation energy, band gap, bulk modulus, and shear modulus, achieving errors comparable to or better than density‑functional‑theory uncertainties.

A unified free‑energy MEGNet model that incorporates temperature, pressure, and entropy as global state inputs predicts U₀, U, H, and G with a combined mean absolute error of 0.010 eV, comparable to separate single‑property models.

Elemental embedding vectors learned by the crystal formation‑energy MEGNet model reproduce known periodic‑table trends and, when transferred to band‑gap and elastic‑moduli models, reduce their mean absolute errors, improving upon prior machine‑learning approaches.
Ensembling two independently trained three‑block MEGNet models lowers the formation‑energy mean absolute error from 0.028 eV/atom to 0.024 eV/atom.

claim_article.text: Increasing the number of MEGNet blocks improves accuracy for properties that depend on longer‑range interactions, such as zero‑point vibrational energy, electronic spatial extent, and dipole moment.
Graph networks constitute a universal machine‑learning framework that can accurately predict properties for both molecules and crystals.
Increasing the crystal graph radius cut‑off from 4 Å to 6 Å slightly worsens the formation‑energy mean absolute error (to 0.03 eV/atom), confirming the 4 Å cut‑off as near‑optimal.

name.text: Atomic cluster expansion of scalar, vectorial and tensorial properties and including magnetism and charge transfer

claim.text: The atomic cluster expansion (ACE) is generalized to model scalar, vectorial and tensorial atomic properties and to include additional atomic degrees of freedom—species, magnetic moments, and charges—on equal footing with atomic positions.
The derived ACE formulas enable efficient evaluation of forces and magnetic torques.
At the lowest order, the magnetic ACE reproduces a distance‑dependent Heisenberg interaction.

Representing tensors with spherical harmonics yields a dramatically sparser basis, where a rank‑N Cartesian tensor with 3^N components can be represented by (N+1)^2 spherical harmonics (e.g., a 10th‑order tensor requires 121 harmonics instead of 59 049 Cartesian components).
Moments Tensor Potentials (MTP) and the Spectral Neighbor Analysis Potential (SNAP) can be expressed exactly as special cases of the ACE.

Neglecting spin‑orbit coupling forces all magnetic angular momenta to be zero, greatly reducing the number of ACE expansion coefficients, since the magnetic contribution to the cohesive energy is only about 10 % of the total.

claim_article.text: The ACE formulation is invariant under translation, rotation, inversion and permutation of identical atoms.
Although the full magnetic and charge‑transfer ACE contains many parameters, hierarchical ordering of interactions allows robust and systematic fitting to reference data.
Implementing the extended ACE for vectorial, tensorial, magnetic and charge degrees of freedom requires no significantly greater effort than the original scalar ACE implementation.
Because the ACE basis is complete and hierarchical, it can in principle achieve arbitrary accuracy for any scalar, vectorial or tensorial property.

name.text: Linking atomic structural defects to mesoscale properties in crystalline solids using graph neural networks

claim.text: The GNN predicts atomic von Mises stress in polycrystalline graphene with a mean normalized relative error of 5.5% and a maximum error below 7% on a test set of 400 crystals.
The GNN predicts atomic tensile stress in porous graphene membranes under tensile strain with a mean normalized relative error of 4.9% and a maximum error of about 10%.
The GNN reproduces the linear decrease of Young’s modulus with vacancy concentration in porous graphene, matching MD results and yielding the fitted relation E = 823.7 − 5635.6·Cv (GPa).

In polycrystalline aluminum, the GNN predicts atomic potential energy with a mean normalized relative error of 11.0% (maximum ≈13%) and achieves R² = 0.99 for mean potential energy versus grain number.
Including tensile strain as an input node feature enables the GNN to accurately predict stress evolution during loading, reproducing nonlinear strain‑stress curves for porous graphene.
The GNN’s stress predictions are substantially more accurate than on‑the‑fly stress calculations from the force field, which exhibit higher errors.

claim_article.text: The GNN framework generalizes across defect types (grain boundaries, vacancies) and material dimensionalities (2D graphene, 3D aluminum), and to unseen defect configurations in over 10⁶ porous graphene structures, maintaining high prediction accuracy despite being trained on only about 1,200 random samples.

Coupling the GNN with a genetic algorithm efficiently discovers optimal holey graphene designs (e.g., arrow‑shaped hole patterns) that achieve significantly lower stress concentration than suboptimal designs, using only ~800 stress evaluations—an order of magnitude fewer than brute‑force search—and reliably locates the global minimum in most of 1,000 random initializations.

The GNN respects physical constraints, accurately capturing derivative properties such as stress fields that obey underlying physical laws, and predicts global properties (Young’s modulus, total potential energy) that follow known physical relationships and match MD results across different crystalline systems.

The Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation (PNA) GNN model achieves the lowest mean and variance of test mean‑squared error among GCN, GAT, and MPNN (sum and max) variants on the polycrystalline graphene dataset.

name.text: The Joint Automated Repository for Various Integrated Simulations (JARVIS) for data-driven materials design

claim.text: JARVIS-DFT contains approximately 40,000 materials and about 1 million calculated properties.
The integrated JARVIS workflow (DFT → FF → ML) enables rapid screening of materials for high solar‑cell efficiency (SLME) with predictions validated against experimental data.

Machine‑learning models trained on Classical Force‑field Inspired Descriptors (CFID) achieve high predictive accuracy for formation energies, exfoliation energies, band gaps, magnetic moments, refractive indices, dielectric constants, thermoelectric performance, and piezoelectric/infrared modes.
Using the vdW‑DF‑OptB88 functional for all dimensionalities yields accurate lattice parameters and formation energies for both van‑der‑Waals and non‑vdW bonded materials.
The meta‑GGA TBmBJ potential predicts band gaps with accuracy comparable to the hybrid HSE06 functional while requiring up to ten times less computational effort.
Comparisons of JARVIS‑DFT computed formation energies, band gaps, and elastic constants with experimental measurements show acceptable error margins, confirming the database’s predictive reliability.

claim_article.text: Beyond‑DFT methods (HSE06, PBE0, G0W0, DMFT) are generated for a subset of materials to provide higher‑level reference data and enable uncertainty quantification.
JARVIS‑FF includes data for roughly 1,500 materials and about 110 classical force‑fields.
JARVIS‑ML provides around 25 machine‑learning models for predicting material properties.
JARVIS‑Tools implements automatic k‑point convergence protocols that improve the precision of DFT calculations.

name.text: A Foundational Potential Energy Surface Dataset for Materials

claim.text: UMLIPs trained on the MatPES dataset achieve test mean absolute errors in energies that are 4–10 times lower than UMLIPs trained on the larger MPRelax or OMat24 datasets.

Across equilibrium, near‑equilibrium, and molecular‑dynamics property benchmarks, MatPES‑trained UMLIPs match or surpass the performance of models trained on much larger datasets such as OMat24 (≈100 M structures).
Molecular‑dynamics simulations using MatPES‑trained UMLIPs exhibit markedly higher stability, with median termination temperatures up to ~1,900 K, versus ~1,300–1,500 K for MPRelax and OMat24 models.

On near‑equilibrium benchmarks, MatPES UMLIPs significantly improve the prediction of shear modulus (G_VRH) and off‑equilibrium forces while achieving similar bulk‑modulus (K_VRH) and heat‑capacity (C_V) accuracy compared to MPRelax and OMat24 models.
MatPES‑trained UMLIPs produce lower fingerprint distances and comparable or slightly higher formation‑energy errors than MPRelax‑trained models, demonstrating superior structural‑relaxation accuracy.
TensorNet‑MatPES predicts ionic conductivities of Li/Na solid electrolytes with high fidelity (positive R²), whereas TensorNet‑MPF severely overestimates conductivities and yields a negative R².

claim_article.text: The MatPES v2025.1 dataset contains 504,811 structures (434,712 PBE and 387,897 r2SCAN calculations) sampled from a configuration space of ~281 million MD snapshots and ~16 billion atomic environments.
The 2DIRECT sampling workflow yields a data‑efficient dataset that, despite being a fraction of the size of MPRelax, samples a substantially larger region of structural and atomic‑environment space.
The r2SCAN functional provides a more accurate description of interatomic bonding than PBE, leading to improved potential‑energy‑surface quality in the MatPES r2SCAN dataset.

Compared with MPRelax and OMat24, the MatPES PBE dataset exhibits a more Gaussian‑like distribution of cohesive energies per atom and a log‑normal‑like distribution of force magnitudes, indicating a better balance of on‑ and off‑equilibrium structures.

name.text: Materials Design and Discovery with High-Throughput Density Functional Theory: The Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD)

claim.text: The Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD) contains over 200,000 DFT‑calculated crystal structures, including experimental ICSD entries and theoretical prototype structures, and is freely accessible to the scientific community without usage restrictions.
At 0 K and zero pressure, 23 % of the 32,489 ICSD structures in the OQMD are thermodynamically stable according to grand canonical linear programming analysis.
The average error between DFT‑predicted formation energies in the OQMD and experimental values from the SGTE database is 24 meV/atom, with a mean absolute error of 113 meV/atom.
High‑throughput screening identified TiP, LiSiNi₂, and CoSi₂ as the most promising Li‑ion battery anode conversion reactions, offering high capacity, moderate voltage, and low volume expansion.

Among binary metal‑oxide candidates, Al₂O₃ provides the optimal balance of HF‑scavenging tendency, lithiation voltage, gravimetric and volumetric capacities, outperforming other oxides in the four‑dimensional design space.
All eleven experimentally known rare‑earth‑containing Mg‑XL‑XS LPSO systems are correctly predicted to be thermodynamically stable by DFT calculations using OQMD convex hulls.

claim_article.text: DFT screening predicts forty‑one previously unreported rare‑earth‑containing Mg‑XL‑XS ternary systems to be thermodynamically stable LPSO phases, providing new experimental targets.

Calcium and strontium are predicted to form stable (or nearly stable) LPSO precipitates in Mg alloys, offering affordable alternatives to rare‑earth elements, with Ca especially promising in the Mg‑Ca‑Zn system.

A combined heuristic‑plus‑machine‑learning model trained on OQMD ternary formation energies predicts formation energies with a mean absolute error of ~0.11 eV/atom, roughly half the typical DFT‑experiment error.

Applying the heuristic‑ML model to 1.6 million hypothetical ternary compositions identified nine top candidates, of which eight were confirmed by DFT to be new stable compounds (e.g., SiYb₃F₅, Pa₂O(SiO₆)).

name.text: AFLOW: an automatic framework for high-throughput materials discovery

claim.text: AFLOW can automatically calculate a wide suite of physical observables across a large database of structures with minimal human intervention.

AFLOW detects most calculation failures, automatically corrects input parameters, restarts calculations, and can run as a Unix daemon to generate, run, correct, and converge many DFT jobs per day, yielding higher throughput than manual management.
AFLOW provides a standardized definition of Brillouin‑zone integration paths for all 14 Bravais lattices, filling a gap in the literature.
AFLOW reproduces experimental phonon dispersion curves for face‑centered cubic Rhodium, showing excellent agreement with measured data.

AFLOW’s cage‑finding algorithm identifies interstitial sites via a topological method, finding 14 cages (6 octahedral, 8 tetrahedral) that reduce to 5 symmetrically inequivalent positions, with radii of 2.2225 Å (octahedral) and 1.9248 Å (tetrahedral).
AFLOW can automatically generate high‑index surface slabs for complex multicomponent compounds, demonstrated for (001), (110) and (111) slabs of an fcc L10 binary.

claim_article.text: AFLOW can automatically create nanoparticle structures of arbitrary radius and separation, enabling high‑throughput nanoparticle studies.
AFLOW can automatically construct convex hulls for binary alloy systems at zero temperature using formation enthalpies from DFT calculations.
The AFLOW database currently contains approximately 400 experimental prototype structures and several million bcc/fcc/hcp‑derived superstructures.
A hybrid HSE06 calculation for ZnO yields a band gap of 2.48 eV, substantially larger than the LDA/GGA gap of 0.7 eV and the PBE+U gap of 1.82 eV.

name.text: Machine learning a general purpose interatomic potential for silicon

claim.text: The Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) for silicon reproduces density functional theory reference results across a wide range of observable properties, including bulk crystal, liquid, amorphous phases, and point, line, and plane defects.
For bulk elastic constants (B, C11, C12, C44) the GAP model achieves fractional errors of less than 10% relative to DFT, outperforming all other evaluated interatomic potentials.
Surface energies of the (111), (110) and (100) silicon cleavage planes are predicted by GAP with errors of around 2% relative to DFT, which is comparable or better than other potentials.
Formation energies of vacancy and interstitial point defects (hexagonal, tetrahedral, dumbbell) are predicted by GAP within 10% of DFT values, providing uniform accuracy across these defects.

For extrapolative planar defects not included in the training set—specifically the (112) Σ3 grain boundary and unstable stacking fault energies on the (111) shuffle and glide planes—GAP errors remain within 20% of DFT, outperforming other models.
Combining a simple repulsive pair potential with a many‑body SOAP‑kernel term in the GAP framework yields meV‑per‑atom accuracy for silicon energetics.

claim_article.text: The Gaussian process regression framework underlying GAP provides an uncertainty quantification that qualitatively estimates the potential’s accuracy for any given atomic configuration.

Using the GAP model enables simulations that would be prohibitively expensive with DFT, such as finite‑temperature phase‑boundary calculations, liquid self‑diffusivity, amorphous silicon formation by slow quench, and dynamic brittle fracture.

A training database of manageable size, constructed from DFT configurations covering relevant phases and defects, is sufficient to achieve high transferability of the GAP model across diverse silicon configurations.
Benchmark comparisons show that the new GAP model yields lower errors than previous GAP models for silicon.

name.text: Universal Machine Learning Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian for Materials

claim.text: The universal HamGNN model achieves a mean absolute error of 5.4 meV for the real‑space Hamiltonian matrix on the test set after the first round of training.
Fine‑tuning the universal model on a small MOF dataset reduces the Hamiltonian matrix MAE to approximately 3.95 meV.

The universal HamGNN model accurately predicts the energy band structures and charge densities of complex multi‑element crystals (e.g., Hf2Zr9Ta6Ti5Nb5B54, HfTaTiB4MoC4, K3Ba3Li2Al4B6O20F), matching DFT results.
For the disordered solid‑electrolyte Li10Si1.5P1.5S11.5Cl0.5, the universal model predicts an insulating behavior with a band gap of 1.4 eV.

The universal HamGNN model accurately predicts the electronic structure of low‑dimensional systems, including a 1625‑atom MoS2/WS2 twisted bilayer (3.5°) and a C60 cluster, reproducing DFT band structures and HOMO wavefunctions.

High‑throughput screening of 188,722 GeNOME crystals with the universal model identifies 21,973 insulators (3,940 direct‑gap) and 5,109 flat‑band materials, nearly doubling the entries in the Materials Flatband Database.

claim_article.text: Using the universal HamGNN model reduces computational cost by several orders of magnitude compared with DFT (e.g., 0.33 core·hours versus 181 core·hours for a large MOF) while preserving accuracy of band gaps and charge‑density differences.
A two‑step training procedure—first minimizing real‑space Hamiltonian error, then adding orbital‑energy error at random k‑points—is essential to obtain a truly universal Hamiltonian model.

Incorporating orbital‑energy loss in a second fine‑tuning round markedly improves band‑structure predictions, yielding energy bands and Fermi surfaces that closely match DFT calculations for the test set.

The universal HamGNN model generalizes to crystals containing more than five distinct elements and to any element supported by the OpenMX PBE pseudopotential library, effectively covering the entire periodic table.

name.text: Using Deep Learning to Predict Fracture Patterns in Crystalline Solids

claim.text: The ConvLSTM model accurately predicts fracture patterns, crack‑length trends, and both mode‑I (tensile) and mode‑II (shear) loading responses across crystal orientations, closely matching atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, with only a minor discrepancy for the x100 orientation under mode‑II shear.
The model predicts fracture toughness values that are comparable to those obtained from atomistic molecular dynamics simulations.

A model trained exclusively on single‑crystal data generalizes to bicrystal and gradient‑orientation crystals, reproducing MD fracture patterns for small orientation differences, capturing overall crack paths for large orientation differences, and handling arbitrary geometry gradients.
The ConvLSTM approach reduces computational cost dramatically compared with full molecular dynamics simulations, enabling rapid fracture predictions.
Representing molecular dynamics results as image‑based geometric matrices preserves crystal orientation information and allows the neural network to learn spatiotemporal fracture behavior.
The training dataset comprises 14,300 paired geometric‑crack image matrices, and the model exhibits convergent loss during training.

name.text: Flow Matching for Accelerated Simulation of Atomic Transport in Crystalline Materials

claim.text: LiFlow predicts lithium mean‑squared displacement with a Spearman rank correlation of 0.7–0.8 on unseen material compositions, enabling screening of high‑diffusivity electrolytes.

LiFlow achieves speed‑ups of up to ~600,000× over ab initio molecular dynamics (and ~400× over MLIP), predicting a 1 ns trajectory in 48 s for a 2 × 2 × 1 LGPS supercell and 352 s for a 4 × 4 × 4 supercell.
The computational cost of LiFlow scales linearly with the number of atoms (O(n)), in contrast to the cubic scaling (O(n³)) of ab initio molecular dynamics.

Incorporating an adaptive, thermally and chemically conditioned Maxwell–Boltzmann prior markedly lowers mean absolute errors and raises rank correlations for MSD and RDF compared with an isotropic prior; ablation studies show performance degradation without it.
Incorporating the Corrector model reduces RDF mean absolute error and mitigates large‑displacement artifacts, improving MSD prediction across temperatures, especially for hydrogen diffusion.

LiFlow trained on 25 ps ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories can generate stable trajectories up to 1 ns in larger (4 × 4 × 4) supercells, reproducing lithium self‑diffusivity, activation energies, and temperature dependence comparable to long AIMD simulations.

claim_article.text: Within the training temperature range, LiFlow’s predicted diffusivity D* closely matches reference values from Winter and Gómez‑Bombarelli.

A direct regression (Regressor) model yields higher mean‑squared‑displacement errors than the generative LiFlow model, demonstrating the necessity of generative modeling for accurate atomic transport simulation.
When extrapolating to temperatures lower than the training range, LiFlow’s predicted diffusivity D* decreases more slowly than reference data, indicating fictitious diffusive behavior at high 1000/T.
The adaptive prior classifier provides limited benefit at the lowest temperature (600 K), reducing its overall effectiveness under that condition.

name.text: Commentary: The Materials Project: A materials genome approach to accelerating materials innovation

claim.text: The Materials Project database contains computed structural, electronic, and energetic data for over 33,000 inorganic compounds, generated using more than 15 million CPU‑hours of computation.
The Materials Project provides an open RESTful API and a high‑level Python library (pymatgen) that enable programmatic querying and analysis of the full dataset.

The workflow software FireWorks together with the custodian job‑management tool automatically manages high‑throughput DFT calculations, self‑heals failed runs, and applies material‑type‑specific workflows.

Visual warnings are displayed on the Materials Project website for compounds whose calculated oxidation states, cell volumes, or bond lengths deviate significantly from experimental norms, helping users assess data reliability.
Automated validation checks compare calculated oxidation states, cell volumes, and bond lengths against experimental data and flag outliers for user review.

Using Materials Project tools, researchers designed a new class of sodium‑based carbonophosphate compounds, predicted them to be thermodynamically stable, synthesized them hydrothermally, and experimentally confirmed their Li‑ion battery performance after ion exchange.

claim_article.text: High‑throughput computational screening through the Materials Project has screened tens of thousands of compounds and identified promising candidates for solar water splitting, photovoltaics, topological insulators, scintillators, CO₂ capture, piezoelectrics, thermoelectrics, catalysis, hydrogen storage, and Li‑ion batteries, with experimental hits reported in several areas.

The Materials Project aims to reduce the typical 10–20 year timeline for advanced material development by providing large‑scale accurate information, thereby accelerating discovery for clean energy, electronics, and other sectors.

The distribution of chromium coordination environments in oxides derived from the database matches known chemical principles: Cr⁶⁺ prefers tetrahedral (4‑fold) coordination, while Cr³⁺ prefers octahedral (6‑fold) coordination.
The Materials Project website receives several hundred unique page views per day and has registered over 4,000 users from academia, government, and industry.

name.text: Simulating diffusion properties of solid-state electrolytes via a neural network potential: Performance and training scheme

claim.text: The DeePMD model successfully reproduces the superionic behavior of solid-state electrolytes with linear Lithium/Sodium mean squared displacement over time and diffusion coefficient uncertainty of about 20% or smaller, which is precise enough for battery applications.
The DeePMD model provides excellent energy conservation in all tested systems up to 2 ns of NVE dynamics.
For LLZO, the computed activation energies range from 0.2 to 0.22 eV, in very good agreement with experimental values of 0.20-0.21 eV for cubic LLZO.
For LGPS, the computed activation energy is 0.16 eV, which is slightly lower than experimental values (0.22 eV) but in line with previous computational studies (0.17-0.21 eV).
For NASICON, training starting from PFF-MD configurations with 480 atoms achieves convergence during the first training loop with activation energy around 0.2 eV.
For NASICON, training starting from FPMD configurations with 80 atoms fails to converge even after three training loops with activation energies spanning 0.2-0.4 eV.

claim_article.text: Starting the training loop with PFF-MD configurations leads to faster convergence than starting with short FPMD trajectories because larger simulation cells can be used.

Training set cleaning procedures including minimum ion-ion distance cutoff, energy/force outlier removal, and loss condition monitoring are necessary to help the algorithm converge to a physical model.

The proposed training protocol based on augmenting the training set via intermediate molecular dynamics simulations can assess the quality of approximate trajectories and computed physical properties.
Starting the training loop with sufficient data sampling a relevant portion of phase space is important for obtaining generalizable models.

name.text: LEARNING INTER-ATOMIC POTENTIALS WITHOUT EXPLICIT EQUIVARIANCE

claim.text: TransIP achieves SO(3) equivariance through training with a contrastive latent equivariance objective rather than hard-wired equivariant architectural constraints.
A generic unconstrained Transformer can serve as an effective backbone for machine-learned interatomic potentials without explicit equivariance constraints.
TransIP achieves 40% to 60% improvement in performance compared to data augmentation baseline (TransAug) across varying OMol25 dataset sizes.
In the limited data regime (1M samples), TransIP achieves 255 meV/Å force MAE versus 600 meV/Å for TransAug, with force cosine similarity of 0.7 versus 0.44.
TransIP achieves 58 meV/atom energy MAE compared to TransAug's 120 meV/atom at 1M training samples.
TransIP-S and TransIP-M achieve significantly faster inference than eSEN baseline at 160,000 and 70,000 atoms/sec versus 15,000 atoms/sec respectively.

claim_article.text: TransIP-L outperforms eSEN-sm in total energy prediction (1.60 vs 1.89 meV/atom MAE) and is competitive in total force MAE after 80 epochs of training.
TransIP attains comparable performance to state-of-the-art equivariant baselines (eSCN, GemNet-OC) on the OMol25 benchmark for machine-learning force fields.
Lower latent equivariance error is monotonically associated with better model performance across all evaluation metrics.
A 48% reduction in equivariance error from 1M to 4M training examples translates to 40-60% performance improvements, exceeding what would be expected from data scaling alone.

name.text: Generalization of Long-Range Machine Learning Potentials in Complex Chemical Spaces

claim.text: Long-range correction schemes in machine learning interatomic potentials are essential for achieving state-of-the-art accuracy, improving in-distribution performance, and enabling significant gains in transferability to unseen regions of chemical space.

Latent Ewald Summation cannot infer correct partial charges without reference charge labels and frequently predicts charges near zero or opposite in sign to reference values in challenging chemical environments such as MOFs.
CELLI-based models trained with reference charges consistently produce physically meaningful results and exhibit good performance across biased split benchmarks on MOF datasets.
Baseline versions of MACE and Allegro are degenerate with respect to total charge and cannot distinguish between molecules with different charge states without long-range corrections.

Biased train-test splitting strategies including cluster, maximal separation, size, and random splits enable rigorous benchmarking by explicitly testing model performance in significantly different regions of chemical space.
EFA enables modeling of long-range interactions without requiring explicit neighbor cutoffs and outperforms CELLI on most benchmarking subsplits when reference charges are unavailable.

claim_article.text: MACE without long-range correction does not generalize well to out-of-distribution samples, while integration of long-range correction schemes has significant effects on both MACE and Allegro architectures.
Strictly local MLIP models overestimate short-range interactions to compensate for missing or incorrectly modeled long-range contributions.

Metal-organic frameworks present an ideal application for MLIPs because classical force fields lack required accuracy while DFT is too computationally expensive for large unit cells and long timescales.
Increasing the number of message passing steps can lead to overfitting and decreased performance compared to baseline models.

name.text: Scalable Parallel Algorithm for Graph Neural Network Interatomic Potentials in Molecular Dynamics Simulations

claim.text: SevenNet achieves over 80% parallel efficiency in weak-scaling scenarios on a 32-GPU cluster with SiO2 benchmarks.
SevenNet-0 achieves mean absolute errors of 24 meV/atom for energy, 0.067 eV/Å for force, and 0.65 GPa for stress on the test set.
The parallelization algorithm restricts communication range between neighboring processors to the original cutoff radius (rc) rather than rc multiplied by message-passing steps.
Spatial decomposition is a valid parallelization strategy only if the energy can be decomposed into atomic energies, which is key for the linear scalability of GNN-IPs.
SevenNet-0 successfully generated amorphous Si3N4 structure with 112,000 atoms through melt-quench MD simulation, reproducing key structural features matching DFT reference data.
The melt-quench simulation with 112,000 atoms on 8 GPUs demonstrated 0.94 parallel efficiency compared to single-GPU baseline.

claim_article.text: SevenNet-0 shows improvements in energy and force accuracies compared to M3GNet (35 meV/atom, 0.072 eV/Å).
Architecture modifications reduced SevenNet-0 total model parameters from 16.24 million (GNoME) to 0.84 million.
SevenNet exhibits nearly ideal strong-scaling performance as long as GPUs are fully utilized.
Strong-scaling performance significantly declines with suboptimal GPU utilization, particularly for lightweight models or simulations with small numbers of atoms.

name.text: Pushing the limits of unconstrained machine-learned interatomic potentials

claim.text: Unconstrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained on large datasets achieve accuracies on par with state-of-the-art equivariant architectures while maintaining orders-of-magnitude lower computational cost than quantum-mechanical methods.

The PET model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on matbench-discovery benchmark (DAF=6.075, Accuracy=0.977, F1=0.924) and exceeds SOTA on SPICE molecular benchmark across most subsets for both energy and force predictions.
PET-OMAD demonstrates the best overall accuracy in predicting energies and forces on MADBench in almost all cases, with the highest success rate (98.43%) in predicting desorption reactions.

Fine-tuning models pre-trained on OMat24 to the MAD dataset achieves near-converged validation metrics in 30-100 epochs versus 700+ epochs when training from scratch, halving validation energy and force errors and achieving 50% lower test error than training on MAD alone.

Non-conservative (unconstrained) MLIP models consistently show 2-3× theoretical speed-up over their conservative counterparts, with direct force prediction providing additional 2-3× speedup compared to forces computed via automatic differentiation.

The PET architecture scales to 730M parameters (OMat-XL) while maintaining tractable memory usage and computational efficiency due to increased node representation size and unconstrained architecture.

claim_article.text: Conservative PET-OAM models achieve state-of-the-art performance on phonon tasks in matbench-discovery and the best overall accuracy in predicting shear modulus among tested models.

Non-conservative models allow residual asymmetries to drive relaxation toward more stable close-packed structures, unlike equivariant models that remain trapped in symmetric but unstable configurations, though 70% (16%) of final configurations retain symmetry of initial structure with 0.01 Å threshold for conservative (non-conservative) models.

Elastic moduli predictions are very sensitive to the lack of energy conservation in MLIP models, and non-conservative models consistently perform worse on matbench-discovery downstream tasks despite achieving better training and validation accuracies.

Central finite differences can more than halve the error for non-equivariant models on phonon calculations by averaging out inconsistencies between symmetry-equivalent displacements, and O(3)-averaging increases symmetric structures to 77% with symprec 0.01 Å in the non-conservative case.

claim.text: Orb-v3 achieves near state-of-the-art performance across evaluations with at least 10x reduction in latency and 8x reduction in memory compared to alternative MLIPs.
Orb-v3-direct-20 uses only 32.8GB GPU memory for 100,000 atom systems and completes in under half a second, while all baseline methods and conservative models encounter Out Of Memory errors.
Orb-v3-direct-* models are the only universal MLIPs that can compute hundreds of forward passes per second, exceeding one million steps per hour for small systems.
Orb-v3-conservative-inf-omat achieves the highest accuracy for almost all physical property metrics while being faster than any best-performing model currently available in literature.

claim_article.text: Orb-v3 can simulate the carbonic anhydrase II enzyme system with over 20,000 atoms under fully solvated conditions for over 700 ps without unphysical behavior.
Orb-v3 models achieve competitive thermal conductivity prediction (κSRME), demonstrating direct models can yield smooth second- and third-order derivatives of the potential energy surface.
Non-equivariant, non-conservative architectures can accurately model physical properties including those requiring higher-order derivatives of the potential energy surface.
Equigrad regularization improves rotational invariance of Orb-v3 by approximately 5x compared to default loss training.
